The temple smelled of tallow smoke and old stone, a darkness so complete that the torches seemed to illuminate nothing beyond their own small radius of orange light. Carved figures watched from the walls—gods or demons, it was impossible to tell which, their stone faces worn smooth by centuries of incense and unanswered prayers.

The priest moved without hurry. His robes, the color of dried blood, made no sound against the stone floor as he crossed to the altar. He was an old man, but his hands did not shake. They had done this many times before, and his body had long since stopped asking questions his mind had answered decades ago.

The altar itself was black basalt, channeled with grooves worn deep by centuries of use, dark stains permanently set into the stone like the rings of some terrible tree. The bound figure upon it had stopped struggling some time ago, exhaustion and terror having burned through whatever fight remained.

The priest lifted the blade—obsidian, edged sharper than steel, catching what little light existed and giving none of it back. He examined it the way a craftsman might examine a tool before work, checking the edge, the balance, nothing more.

He spoke the words required of him. They were old words, worn smooth like the stone faces above, and his voice carried no more weight than if he were reciting a tax ledger. There was no cruelty in his tone, no reverence either. Only the flat cadence of ritual performed ten thousand times, the words having long since been emptied of any meaning they might once have held for him.

The cut, when it came, was precise. Economical. He had learned exactly how much pressure was required, exactly where the blade needed to travel, and he wasted no motion beyond what was necessary. The sound that followed was wet and final. He did not flinch from it. He did not look away, nor did he look with any particular attention—his eyes were the eyes of a man checking that a task had been completed correctly, nothing more.

Blood ran into the carved channels, finding the paths worn for it by ten thousand sacrifices before this one, pooling in the basin beneath with a sound like rain beginning. The priest set down the blade and reached for the ceremonial bowl, his movements unhurried, methodical, the movements of someone who had stopped seeing the body in front of him as anything other than the next step in a sequence he had performed since before some of the younger acolytes had been born.

The alley tilts sideways, or maybe that's just me.

I'm sitting against the brick wall now—don't remember deciding to sit, just found myself here, legs splayed out in front of me like they belong to someone else. My hand is pressed against my side where the wetness keeps coming, warm at first, but that warmth is leaving now too, like everything else.

The streetlight above me hums and flickers. I watch it instead of looking down at myself. Easier that way. The light is orange, then white, then orange again, and each time it dims I think *there it goes* but it always comes back. I wonder which time it won't.

My heartbeat is the loudest thing in the world. I can hear it in my ears, a wet thudding that used to be background noise, the kind of thing you forget you have. Now it's everything. *Thud. Thud.* Too fast. Then—is it slowing? I can't tell anymore if it's slowing down or if I'm just getting used to the rhythm, the way you stop hearing a clock after a while.

The cold started in my fingers. Strange, since the night isn't cold at all—I remember sweating earlier, before all this, when it was just words and posturing and the glint of something metal catching the light. Now my fingers are ice and the cold is climbing up my wrists, into my arms, patient as rising water.

I try to call out. My voice comes out smaller than I expect, swallowed by the alley, by the hum of the streetlight, by the distant sound of a car passing somewhere that might as well be another world.

The light flickers again. Longer this time. The dark presses in at the edges like something curious, testing whether I'll notice.

*Thud.*

I think about stupid things. A song from when I was a kid. The smell of my mother's kitchen. The fact that I never called her back this week, and now I won't.

*Thud.*

The cold has reached my chest. It's almost peaceful, if I let it be. Like sinking into water that's been warm and now is just... still. Still water.

The streetlight is mostly dark now. Just an orange ember of itself, far away, like a star I'm falling from.

*Thud.*

I want to be angry. I want to be afraid. But there's only this heaviness, this quiet, the alley going soft and grey at the edges. My own heartbeat sounds far away now, like it's already left without me, already turned the corner down the street.

*Thud.*

I close my eyes. Or maybe they were already closed. I can't tell anymore where I end and the dark begins.

*Thud...*

The silence after is the loudest thing of all.

# The Note

Detective Sarah Voss pulled on a fresh pair of gloves before stepping into the child's bedroom. The forensics team had already cleared out, leaving behind only their chalk marks and the faint smell of fingerprint powder. Stuffed animals lined a shelf above the bed, arranged with unsettling precision, like an audience.

The note sat on the desk, found tucked beneath a math workbook. The handwriting was careful—too careful, each letter formed with the kind of deliberate control that came from practice, not childhood clumsiness.

She read it twice before she let herself believe what it said.

*Buttons wouldn't stop looking at me wrong.*

*I know dogs can't really do that on purpose but he did. Every time I came in the room his eyes would follow me and I knew he was telling the others. Mom says I imagine things but I don't imagine the way he watched. He was going to tell. I don't know what he was going to tell but I felt it, the telling, like a itch behind my eyes.*

*I didn't want to. I want everyone to know I didn't want to but he gave me no choice. You can't let things watch you forever. Eventually you have to make them stop.*

*I held him for a long time after. He felt softer than before. I don't know why that surprised me.*

*I'm not sorry exactly. I'm sorry that I had to but not sorry I did it. Those are different. Mom doesn't understand the difference but I think someone will.*

*Maybe you.*

Voss set the note down and stared at the wall for a long moment, the quiet of the room pressing against her ears. Outside, she could hear the mother crying softly in the hallway, a sound like something tearing.

She thought about the careful handwriting. The audience of stuffed animals. *Maybe you.*

She picked up her radio. "I need a child psychologist down here," she said. "Now."

---

The corridor stank of diesel and fear before Marek even pulled the trigger.

He'd taken the doorway low, shoulder against the frame, the weight of the tank dragging at his back like a second spine. Six of them in the room beyond—he'd counted through the gap before kicking it open. Crates for cover. Rifles already swinging toward the sound.

He didn't give them time to use them.

The igniter caught with a cough, then a roar, and the world in front of him turned orange. The flamethrower didn't just burn—it *threw*, a ribbon of fire unspooling across the room like something alive, hungry, looking for a place to land. It found the nearest man first. He didn't even get a scream out before the fire wrapped him, just a strangled grunt and then the sound—God, the sound—of fat hissing, fabric curling back from skin in blackened ribbons.

Then the screaming started.

It wasn't human, not really. It was something older than language, something that came up from the gut and didn't stop until the lungs gave out from the smoke instead of the noise. Marek swept the nozzle in a slow arc, feeling the heat radiate back at him even through the suit—a wall of it, pressing against his face like he'd opened an oven door and stuck his head inside. His eyes watered. Sweat ran into them anyway.

The smell hit a second later, riding in under the cordite and diesel: a thick, greasy sweetness, like meat left too long on a grill, except wrong, except *wet*, except mixed with the stink of melting plastic from gear straps and boot soles. It coated the inside of his nose. He'd tasted it before. He'd never gotten used to it.

One man tried to run, a living torch staggering between the crates, slapping at himself like that would do anything, like his hands weren't already cooking. He went down near the far wall, twitching, the fire eating through his jacket into whatever was underneath, and the twitching slowed, and then it didn't move at all, just smoked, gently, obscenely, like a cigarette left burning in an ashtray.

Marek kept the trigger down a beat longer than he needed to. The flame guttered, caught, painted the walls black. Somewhere under the roar he could still hear one of them—the last one—wheezing out something that might have been a prayer or might have just been air escaping a ruined throat.

Then it stopped.

He released the trigger. The flame died to a thread, then nothing, and the silence that came after was almost worse than the screaming—just the crackle of small fires catching on whatever fabric and paper had been left scattered around, and the soft, awful sound of fat still rendering off bone.

Marek stood in the doorway a moment, breathing through his mouth, letting the smoke clear enough to see.

Six. Done.

He shouldered the tank higher, stepped over what was left of the nearest man, and moved on to the next room.

# The Shedding

Marcus first noticed it in the shower, three weeks after the bite that wouldn't heal. A patch of skin on his forearm had gone gray and papery, like old parchment left too long in the sun. When he scratched it, it came away in his fingers—not bleeding, just *peeling*, revealing something dark and glistening underneath.

By the second week of October, the shedding had spread to his chest and back. He'd wake to find curls of his former self scattered across the sheets like discarded wrapping paper, thin as onion skin, still bearing the faint outline of the tattoo he'd gotten at nineteen. The new skin beneath was darker, tighter, stretched over muscle that seemed to shift and bunch in ways that didn't match his anatomy textbooks.

The bones came next, and these nights he learned to muffle his screams with a pillow. His spine would seize first—a deep, grinding ache that built until something inside simply *gave*, vertebrae popping like knuckles cracked in sequence. He'd feel his ribs splay outward, cartilage softening and reforming into something with more curve, more room. His jaw unhinged itself one Tuesday while he was alone in his apartment, dropping with a wet click that he felt more than heard, before slowly, agonizingly, reassembling into a longer, narrower shape. He vomited afterward, but what came up wasn't food.

It was the smaller changes that frightened him most—not the obvious horrors, but the quiet erosions. He stopped flinching when he stepped on the neighbor's cat, mid-transformation, his new and heavier foot crushing it without him quite meaning to. He noticed but didn't *feel* the absence of guilt, the way you might notice a missing tooth with your tongue—an absence, a hollow space where something used to be.

He used to call his mother every Sunday. Now the thought of her voice produced nothing—not love, not duty, just a calculation: *is this useful*. He watched himself stop caring with the same detached curiosity he'd once reserved for nature documentaries. Empathy didn't disappear all at once. It thinned, like the skin, like something being prepared to be shed and left behind.

The final piece of him that remained human was a single, persistent thought, growing fainter each day: *I should be afraid of what I'm becoming.*

By November, he'd stopped having that thought at all. He simply *was*, in the way a storm simply is—no malice, no doubt, just hunger and the growing, glorious freedom of having nothing left to lose.

# Five Minutes

The fluorescent light hummed overhead. Marcus sat on the edge of the cot, hands folded, while the man in the gray uniform stood by the door, keys still in hand though he hadn't used them yet.

"You're early," Marcus said.

"Warden wanted me to walk you down myself. Said I've done enough of these." The executioner—Daniel, though few inmates ever learned his name—remained by the door.

"Have you? Done enough?"

"Eleven, counting tonight."

Marcus laughed, a dry sound. "Does it get easier?"

"No. It gets quieter. That's different from easier."

Silence settled between them. Marcus looked at his hands.

"I keep thinking I should feel more," he said. "Afraid, or sorry, or something. Mostly I just feel tired."

"That's common. People expect lightning bolts. Mostly it's just—" Daniel paused, searching. "Mostly it's just a Tuesday that happens to be the last one."

"That's bleak."

"You asked."

Marcus almost smiled. "Can I ask you something else? Do you believe I did it?"

Daniel was quiet for a moment. "Doesn't matter what I believe. Twelve people decided. That's not my job."

"But you must have an opinion."

"I stopped having opinions about that a long time ago. I have an opinion about how this is done. That it's done right. Quick. No theater."

"Small mercies."

"They're not small to the person they're given to."

The clock on the wall ticked. Three minutes now.

"I have a daughter," Marcus said. "She's twelve. She wrote me a letter last week. Didn't read it yet. Couldn't."

Daniel said nothing, but he didn't look away either.

"What do I do with that?" Marcus asked. "Five minutes left and there's a letter from my kid I haven't read."

"You could read it now."

"And then what? Walk out of here crying?"

"You could walk out of here however you want. That part's still yours."

Marcus pulled a folded paper from his pocket—he'd had it on him the whole time. His hands shook slightly as he opened it.

He read silently. Daniel watched the floor, giving him that much privacy in a room with no privacy left.

When Marcus finished, his eyes were wet but his voice was steady. "She says she forgives me. Says it like it's simple."

"Maybe for her it is."

"How do I carry that in five minutes?"

"You don't carry it," Daniel said. "You just let it be the last thing you know."

Marcus folded the letter carefully, placed it on the cot like he was leaving it for someone. "Will you make sure she gets this back? The letter?"

"Yes."

A guard's voice came faintly from down the hall. Time.

Marcus stood. His legs held, though barely.

"Daniel," he said—first time he'd used the name. "Thank you for not pretending this is okay."

"It's not okay. It's just what's happening."

"Yeah."

They walked toward the door together, the keys finally turning in the lock, the corridor stretching out long and white and quiet ahead of them.

The first sound was the worst—dirt hitting wood, a hollow drumbeat that meant the world above had decided to close.

*Thud.*

Mara's fingers found the satin lining of the lid six inches above her face. Six inches. She'd measured it a hundred times already in the dark, as if the measurement might change, might stretch into something survivable.

*Thud. Thud.*

They were going fast. Of course they were going fast—nobody likes to linger at a graveside, even when they don't know they've made a mistake, even when the woman they're burying is still warm, still breathing, still screaming behind a sedative that had only mimicked death instead of bringing it.

She tried to scream now. It came out as a wet, swollen sound, barely louder than her own heartbeat slamming in her ears. The air already tasted used, tasted like her own breath recycled, thickened with the smell of new wood and the cheap polyester of her burial dress.

*Thud.*

She thought about how much air six feet of pine box might hold. She'd read somewhere—some lifetime ago, in some context that had seemed merely interesting and not urgently, personally vital—that a person could survive maybe five or six hours in a sealed coffin before the oxygen gave out. But that math assumed stillness, assumed calm, and her heart was a fist against her ribs, her lungs already dragging for more than they were getting.

She pushed against the lid. It didn't move, of course it didn't move, there were probably already inches of earth settling on top of it, and even if there weren't, even if it was just her against the wood, she didn't have the leverage, didn't have the room to gather any force. Her elbows banged her own sides. Her knees couldn't bend without striking the walls. The space that had seemed, in the dim panic of waking, like a coffin-shaped absence of hope, was actually smaller than that—was a mold of her own body, a mute insistence that she stay exactly as she'd been arranged.

*Thud. Thud. Thud.*

Faster now. Or maybe that was just her perception warping, time stretching and compressing as the carbon dioxide built in the small cave of her skull. She pressed her palms flat against the lid and pushed until her shoulders screamed, until she understood with her body what her mind already knew: this was not a door. This had never been built to open from the inside.

The thuds blurred together into something almost rhythmic, almost like rain, and she thought, absurdly, that whoever was shoveling must be tired by now, must want this over as much as she did, though for entirely different reasons.

Her breathing had gone ragged, shallow, fast—too fast, drinking the air too quickly, and some clinical corner of her mind noted this even as the rest of her couldn't stop. *Slow down,* she told herself. *Slow down or you'll use it all.* But the body does not listen to reason when it believes it is dying. The body only grasps, only claws, only wants more, now, immediately, before the wanting itself becomes the thing that kills her.

The sounds from above grew muffled. Distant. Each shovelful landing with less and less audible violence, as though the dirt itself were growing softer, or her ears were closing along with everything else.

She stopped pushing. Not because she'd given up—though some treacherous, exhausted part of her had—but because there was no more air to spend on effort. She needed what little remained for breathing. Just breathing. The most basic animal task, suddenly the only task, the only thing left to do with the minutes she might or might not have.

In the dark, with her eyes open onto nothing, she found herself counting heartbeats instead of shovel-falls, because the shovel had gone silent, because someone, somewhere above, had decided enough dirt covered her, decided the job was done, decided—without knowing, without choosing it, but deciding all the same—that this was where she would stay.

The last sound she heard wasn't dirt at all.

It was her own pulse, slowing, growing distant, like footsteps walking away across packed earth.

# The Conversion Ward

The fluorescent lights hummed at a frequency designed to keep patients docile, though Mira had stopped fighting the restraints hours ago. Not from compliance—from exhaustion. The straps had cut grooves into her wrists that wouldn't fully heal, not anymore, not after what they'd already taken.

Dr. Voss moved between the rows of tables like a man inspecting livestock, which, in the Ministry's terminology, wasn't far from accurate. "Unit 7-Delta," he read from his tablet, not looking at her face. "Respiratory conversion, phase two."

The first phase had taken her left lung six weeks ago, replaced it with something that clicked when she breathed—a small mechanical sound like a clock that never quite kept time. She'd screamed for three days afterward, not from the surgery itself (they were efficient with anesthesia, at least), but from waking to find she could no longer cry properly. The tear ducts had been "optimized for efficiency," whatever that meant. Now her eyes just burned, dry and useless, when grief came.

"Phase two," Voss continued, "diaphragm replacement. You'll find breathing requires no conscious effort afterward. More efficient for labor quotas."

*I don't want to breathe efficiently,* she tried to say. *I want to breathe like a person, even badly, even when it hurts.* But the speech modulator they'd installed in her throat during the first procedure converted her words into something flatter, stripped of inflection—a voice-shaped void where her voice used to be.

What emerged was: "Acknowledged."

The technicians arrived with their tools that looked less like scalpels now and more like soldering irons, like the equipment her father once used in his workshop before the Ministry repurposed all workshops for the Conversion Program. She remembered—did she still remember, or was this another thing they'd let her keep as a control measure?—sitting on his lap while he fixed radios, his hands rough and warm and entirely human.

Her hands now had calibrated grip strength. Optimal for assembly line work. She could no longer feel the difference between silk and sandpaper.

The pain when they began was not the searing, animal pain of the first surgery. They'd learned to modulate that, to keep subjects conscious but manageable, productive even during their own dismantling. This pain was different—a deep, electric wrongness, as if her body were being rewritten in a language it didn't speak. She felt the moment they disconnected the old diaphragm, the muscle that had moved with her sobs, her laughter, her first nervous breath before kissing someone she'd loved. Gone. Replaced by a bellows-mechanism that would breathe for her, indifferent to joy or sorrow, simply maintaining oxygen levels at Ministry-specified parameters.

Through the haze, she caught her reflection in the surgical lamp's curved surface—a woman's face, still recognizably hers, but the eyes had changed. Not the color or shape, but something behind them. The Ministry called it "stabilization." Mira, in the last moments she'd still call herself that name, understood it differently: 

*They aren't removing our pain. They're removing what makes pain mean anything.*

A person could grieve the loss of a lung. A machine simply registered decreased capacity and adjusted output accordingly. She could feel herself sliding from the former category to the latter, not all at once but in increments, each surgery a small death disguised as an upgrade.

"Vitals stable," a technician reported. "Proceeding with diaphragm integration."

In the bed beside her, Unit 7-Charlie—formerly someone named Tomas, she thought, from the resistance cell that had failed six months ago—lay motionless, his chest cavity open, exposing the brushed-steel mechanism that had replaced his heart. He didn't scream anymore. He hadn't screamed in weeks. Whether that meant he'd transcended the pain or simply lost the part of himself capable of recognizing it as pain, she couldn't say.

She wondered, as the anesthesia began its slow crawl through her veins, which fate awaited her.

She wondered if she'd still be able to wonder, after.

The lights buzzed on, indifferent, efficient, and the machines began their careful, patient work of erasing what remained of the woman who used to dream of summer rain on skin that could still feel it.

# The Geometry of Endings

Detective Elena Vasquez had stopped telling people about the beauty six months ago, after her partner looked at her like she'd suggested something obscene. But she still saw it—couldn't unsee it, really—every time she crossed a new threshold of police tape.

It wasn't that she enjoyed the violence. She understood, intellectually, the tragedy each scene represented: a life extinguished, a family shattered. But her eyes, trained over fifteen years to find patterns in chaos, had started finding something else entirely. Symmetry. Intention. The accidental artistry of catastrophe.

The Hendricks scene was the one that finally cracked something open in her.

The victim lay in his study, and for a long moment, Elena simply stood in the doorway, unable to move forward. Morning light fell through the gauze curtains at a precise diagonal, catching the floating particles of dust disturbed by the struggle, transforming them into something like gold leaf suspended in amber. The blood had pooled beneath him in a shape that, viewed from the doorway, evoked the wings of some dark bird taking flight from his chest.

She made herself catalog the details professionally, the way she'd been trained.

*Victim, male, approximately fifty-five years. Single laceration, defensive wounds on forearms.*

But her mind kept sliding sideways into different language. The way his right hand had fallen open, fingers curled like a sleeping child's. The bookshelf behind him, undisturbed, spines creating vertical lines that framed the scene like a proscenium. Even the disarray—papers scattered from his desk—seemed to follow some hidden logarithmic spiral, white rectangles against dark wood.

She photographed the wound pattern and found herself adjusting her angle not for forensic clarity, but for composition. The way the light caught the wound's edge. The contrast of red against the pale blue of his shirt—a blue she recognized, suddenly, as nearly identical to a particular sky in a Vermeer painting she'd seen once in Amsterdam.

*This is wrong,* she thought, even as she crouched lower, chasing the perfect angle. *This is a person. This was someone's father.*

But the thought arrived and dissolved like sugar in rain, washed away by the next observation: how the blood had found the grain of the wood floor and followed it, creating thin tributaries that branched and re-branched with the same fractal patience as a river delta seen from space, or the veins of a leaf held up to light.

Her colleague Martinez called her name. She didn't answer immediately. She was looking at the dead man's other hand, the one resting on a closed book—and seeing, despite herself, despite everything she knew about right and wrong, the way it looked like a study for a Renaissance painting. *The reading interrupted.* *Memento mori.* Her mind reached for these references the way other detectives reached for procedure manuals.

"Vasquez." Martinez's voice carried an edge now. "You've been standing there for ten minutes."

She blinked, and the spell fractured slightly, enough for guilt to seep through the cracks. She thought of the man's family, who would arrive at the morgue not to admire compositional balance, but to identify a husband, a father, a person who had laughed and worried and loved imperfectly, like everyone does.

"Sorry," she said. "Cataloging."

But even as she said it, she was already wondering if her camera had captured the way the light fell. Already wondering if anyone else would ever see what she saw—this terrible, undeniable beauty, blooming like something poisonous in the wreckage of an ordinary man's last morning.

She didn't know, yet, that this was the case that would break her. That somewhere between the wound pattern's elegant arc and the golden hour light, she had stopped being able to tell the difference between witnessing and consuming. That the next time someone asked her to describe what she saw at a scene, the words that would come out wouldn't be about evidence at all.

She only knew, standing there, that she needed to stay a moment longer. Just to look. Just to see.

The dust motes turned slowly in the light, indifferent to her hunger, indifferent to everything except the law of falling, the simple poetry of things finding their way, eventually, to ground.

But her mind kept sliding sideways into different language. The way his right hand had fallen open, fingers curled like a sleeping child's. The bookshelf behind him, undisturbed, spines creating vertical lines that framed the scene like a proscenium. Even the disarray—papers scattered from his desk—seemed to follow some hidden logarithmic spiral, white rectangles against dark wood.

The contrast of red against the pale blue of his shirt—a blue she recognized, suddenly, as nearly identical to a particular sky in a Vermeer painting she'd seen once in Amsterdam.

This is wrong, she thought, even as she crouched lower, chasing the perfect angle. This is a person. This was someone's father.

She was looking at the dead man's other hand, the one resting on a closed book—and seeing, despite herself, despite everything she knew about right and wrong, the way it looked like a study for a Renaissance painting. The reading interrupted. Memento mori. Her mind reached for these references the way other detectives reached for procedure manuals.

She blinked, and the spell fractured slightly, enough for guilt to seep through the cracks. The rope had been thrown over the cottonwood's lowest branch an hour before noon, and by the time the sun stood directly overhead, Caleb Marsh had nothing left to say.

The men held him steady on the borrowed horse, its skin twitching at flies, indifferent to the weight it carried. Caleb's hands were bound behind him, the rope at his wrists worn slick with sweat. He'd stopped cursing them somewhere around the second hour of waiting. Now he just stared at the horizon like a man trying to memorize it.

"Anything you want said over you?" the foreman asked, not unkindly.

Caleb shook his head.

The noose had been set with care—thirteen wraps, the way old Pruitt had taught them, a man who'd done this before and took a grim pride in doing it right. They slid it down over Caleb's collar and drew it snug beneath his left ear.

Nobody spoke the word *ready*. Somebody just slapped the horse's flank, hard, and it bolted out from under him.

The drop wasn't long, but it didn't need to be. There came a sound like a green branch stepped on underfoot—a wet, snapping crack—and Caleb's whole body jerked taut against the rope, then hung still for the span of a breath.

Then it started. Not the man, not anymore, but the body—legs kicking out in a ragged, senseless rhythm, boot heels scraping at empty air. His shoulders rolled. His bound hands flexed once, fingers spreading wide, then curling into fists. It went on longer than any of them wanted to watch—a minute, maybe more—the rope creaking against the branch, the body twisting slow one way and then slow back, like something hung up to dry.

The foreman looked away first. Most of them did, eventually, finding something else to study—the horse cropping grass a few yards off, the dust on their boots, the white sky. Only Pruitt watched it through to the end, arms crossed, face carved out of nothing.

When it was finally still, the only sound left was the rope's slow groan against the bark, and the wind moving through the leaves overhead like it hadn't noticed a thing.

The fog rolled through the alley like something alive, curling around broken crates and rusted fire escapes. Marguerite pressed herself into the shadows, watching the young man stumble from the bar's side entrance, his keys jangling uselessly in fingers too drunk to find the lock of his car.

The hunger had been building for three days now—a hollow, gnawing thing that lived beneath her ribs, that turned every pulse she heard on the street into a kind of music. She could hear his heart from here, thudding with the particular rhythm of alcohol and exhaustion. Slow. Trusting. Unaware.

She moved without sound, the way water moves around stone.

"You look lost," she said, and he turned, swaying, his eyes catching on her face the way men's eyes always did—pulled in before they understood why.

"M'fine," he mumbled. "Jus' need air."

She closed the distance between them in the time it took him to blink. Her hand found the back of his neck, gentle, almost tender, as she guided him toward the brick wall. He didn't resist. They rarely did, not at first—there was something in her gaze that unspooled the will like thread from a spool.

"This won't hurt," she lied, and tilted his head to the side.

The hunger sharpened into something unbearable, a white-hot wire drawn taut through her chest. She could smell the blood beneath his skin, rich and warm, calling to the ancient thing in her that had no name anymore, only need.

Her teeth broke skin with two sounds—a soft tear, then his gasp, sharp and startled, more confusion than pain. Twin punctures bloomed red at his throat, and she drank.

The first pull was always the worst—too fast, too desperate, the hunger overriding the discipline of centuries. She forced herself to slow, to savor, though his pulse was already faltering beneath her mouth, stuttering like a candle in wind.

His hands found her shoulders, weak protest, fingers curling into her coat and then sliding loose as his strength bled out of him in time with the blood leaving his veins. His breathing grew shallow, ragged. His knees buckled, and she held him up with one arm, the way one might hold a sleeping child.

"Please," he whispered, the word barely audible, more breath than sound.

She paused, just long enough to look at his face—pale now, lips losing their color, eyes glassy and unfocused, struggling to find hers and failing.

The hunger told her to finish. The hunger always told her to finish.

She drank until his pulse slowed to something thin and thready, until his body had gone slack and cold-edged in her arms, and only then did she pull back, dragging her tongue once across the wounds to seal them, an old mercy that cost her nothing.

She lowered him to the pavement, propped against a stack of crates, his chest rising and falling in shallow, uneven breaths. He would wake in an hour, dizzy, anemic, his memory of her already dissolving like sugar in rain.

Marguerite wiped her mouth with the back of her hand and looked up at the sliver of moon caught between rooftops.

The hunger was quiet now. For a little while, at least.

# The Hollow

The first cut came across her shoulder blade, a line of fire that bloomed before she even heard the sound—a wet, tearing whisper through the air. Mara spun, knife raised against nothing. Just trees. Just the gray afternoon light filtering through leaves that shouldn't have looked so peaceful.

Blood ran warm down her spine, soaking into her shirt, and she pressed her back against the nearest trunk, breathing hard, eyes raking the empty space around her.

*Where. Where. Where.*

The forest gave no answers. No silhouette, no shadow that moved wrong, no telltale bend of grass beneath unseen weight. Just her own ragged breathing and the small, insistent throb spreading from the wound, sharp and clean as a paper cut scaled up to something obscene.

She heard it before she felt it the second time—a soft displacement of air, like a held breath being released right next to her ear. She threw herself sideways and still it caught her, a line of agony opening across her forearm as she raised it instinctively. The pain was strange: not the dull crush of a fist, not the bright shock of a fall, but something exact and deliberate, like being unmade with surgical precision.

She didn't scream. Screaming felt like giving it something.

Her mind scrambled for logic—*air pressure, wind, something with claws that bends light*—but logic was a luxury she couldn't afford with her blood pattering onto dead leaves in twin rhythms now, shoulder and arm both weeping in time with her pulse.

She ran. Branches whipped her face, real branches, solid and known, almost a relief in their physicality. Behind her—beside her—she couldn't tell—the air hissed again. She juked left on instinct and felt the wind of the strike pass close enough to stir her hair, missing her by the width of a held thought.

That was the worst part. Not the pain, though the pain was bad—a deep, insistent burning that made her left arm feel half-numb, fingers tingling, blood slicking her grip on the knife she still couldn't aim at anything. The worst part was the *absence*. Every instinct she had, every animal sense honed by millions of years of evolution to spot the predator, the rustle, the eyes in the dark—all of it found nothing. Her body screamed *there is no threat* even as her shoulder screamed otherwise, even as fresh agony lanced across her calf and she went down hard onto one knee.

She was being erased a piece at a time by something that left no mark on the world except the marks it left on her.

She twisted, slashing wildly with the knife, and for one heartbeat—one impossible heartbeat—she felt resistance. The blade caught on something that gave like flesh, and she heard, for the first time, a sound that wasn't her own ragged breath: a low, wet exhale, almost amused.

Then it was gone again, and so was the feeling in her left hand, and she understood, with the particular clarity of someone who has run out of time to be afraid in any abstract way, that whatever was hunting her had only ever been toying with the idea of letting her see it.

The grass beside her bent down, slow and deliberate, under a weight she would never see arrive.

The fluorescent light buzzed overhead, too bright, too white, casting everything in a sickly glare that made the blood already on the floor look black instead of red.

Marcus stood with his hands bound behind him, but they hadn't touched his mouth. That was the cruelty of it. They wanted him to speak.

"One," the man in the gray suit said again, almost bored. He checked his watch. "You have thirty seconds before I choose for you, and trust me, I won't choose kindly."

Three people knelt in front of him. Sarah, mascara streaked down her face in dark rivers, lips moving in silent prayer or pleading, he couldn't tell which. Dale, who had stopped crying ten minutes ago and now just stared at the floor with the particular stillness of someone who had already left his body. And Priya, who was looking directly at Marcus, her eyes clear and terrible in their steadiness, as if she already knew what he would say and was trying to make it easier.

"I can't," Marcus said. His voice came out wrong, cracked down the middle.

"Twenty seconds."

He thought about Sarah's kids, two of them, ages six and nine, waiting at home for a mother who read them stories with funny voices for each character. He thought about Dale's mother, alone now since his father died last spring, how Dale called her every single Sunday without fail. He thought about Priya, who had no one, who had told him once in a moment of late-night honesty that he and the others were the only family she'd managed to keep.

That she had no one made it worse, somehow. Like her aloneness was a wound already there, and choosing her would just be widening it.

"Fifteen."

"This isn't—you can't ask me to—" 

"I'm not asking. I'm telling. Someone dies in the next ten seconds. The only variable is whether you have any say in who."

Sarah was openly sobbing now. Dale hadn't moved. Priya held his gaze and very slightly, almost imperceptibly, shook her head—not pleading, not begging him to save her, but something else. Permission, maybe. Or refusal to let him carry the full weight alone.

"Five."

The word tore out of him before he'd fully decided, before his mind caught up to whatever animal calculation had happened in his gut: "Me. Take me instead."

The man in the gray suit smiled, and it was the smile of someone who'd heard this exact plea a hundred times and found it equally unmoving each time. "Not an option. Three."

"Dale," Marcus whispered. "God forgive me. Dale."

He didn't choose Dale because Dale deserved it less than the others, or because he weighed lives like currency and found Dale's worth less. He chose Dale because Dale had already gone somewhere else in his mind, because some terrible mercy told him that Dale, of the three, might already be beyond the reach of this particular horror.

He would spend the rest of his life unsure if that was love or cowardice.

The gunshot was very loud in the small concrete room, and then it was over, and the silence after was worse than the sound itself had been—a silence with a body-shaped hole in it. Sarah made a sound like something breaking. Priya closed her eyes, just once, slow, and when she opened them she was looking at Marcus still, and there was no forgiveness in her face, but there wasn't condemnation either. Just the unbearable fact of being alive when someone else wasn't, and the knowledge that they would carry this room inside them for whatever remained of their lives, however long or short that might now be.

Marcus didn't look away from Dale's body. He made himself memorize it—the angle of the collapse, the spreading dark stain, the absolute absence where a person had been seconds before. He owed it that much, at least. To not look away from what his voice had done.

The man in the gray suit was already checking his watch again, as if a man's life were a brief interruption to his schedule.

"Now," he said. "Let's discuss the next room."

The garage light had been on for three nights straight.

Marcus noticed these things now—small inconsistencies in the rhythm of a street he'd lived on for eleven years. Gerald Voss had always been the kind of neighbor you forgot existed: quiet, polite in the way of someone reciting lines, mowing his lawn every Saturday at exactly nine. But the garage light, and the new padlock on the side door, and the way Gerald had flinched when Marcus mentioned the missing Hendricks girl from two streets over—these were splinters under a fingernail. Small. Persistent. Impossible to ignore once you'd felt them.

He told himself he was being paranoid. He told himself this right up until the night he saw Gerald dragging something heavy-wrapped in a tarp toward the storm cellar at 2 a.m., moving with the careful, practiced economy of a man who had done this before.

Marcus didn't call the police. He should have. Instead, three nights later, when Gerald's car pulled out for what Marcus had learned was a standing Thursday night errand, he crossed the strip of grass between their houses with a flashlight and a feeling like ice water in his chest.

The cellar door was unlocked. That detail would bother him later—the carelessness of it, or maybe the confidence.

The stairs went down further than he expected, the air growing cold and mineral, like the inside of a cave. At the bottom, his flashlight beam caught a door that didn't belong in a suburban basement: reinforced steel, the kind you'd see on a bank vault, incongruous against the unfinished concrete around it.

It wasn't locked either.

The smell hit him first—chemical and sweet and wrong, the smell of a butcher shop crossed with a hospital. Then the light switch, which he found by instinct, flooding the room in a fluorescent hum.

Marcus would spend the rest of his life trying not to remember what the light revealed.

Shelves lined three walls, the kind you'd buy for canned goods or tools, except what sat on them had been arranged with the reverence of museum pieces. Glass jars, dozens of them, filled with something preserved in cloudy yellow liquid—he made himself look away before his mind could finish identifying what floated inside. Photographs covered the fourth wall in neat grids, women's faces captured in moments before they understood what was happening to them, their eyes wide with a terror that seemed to leak out of the photo paper itself.

There was a workbench. There were instruments laid out with surgical precision, some of them rust-dark, none of them clean.

And there were the names—handwritten on index cards, pinned beneath each photograph, dates spanning back further than Marcus could process standing there with his stomach trying to climb up through his throat. Seventeen cards. He counted them twice because his mind refused to accept the number the first time.

In the corner, almost an afterthought, sat a child's pink backpack. Hendricks Elementary was stitched along the strap in fading thread.

Marcus heard the car door close upstairs—the specific, ordinary sound of a Honda Civic settling into its frame—and understood with sudden, total clarity that Gerald had come home early.

That he was no longer alone in the house.

That the only way out was the stairs he'd come down, and the only way to those stairs was through whatever waited at the top of them now, footsteps already moving with that same patient, unhurried confidence across the kitchen floor above his head.

# Lockdown

The alarm cut through Cell Block C like a physical thing, klaxons screaming red light across concrete walls already splattered with worse colors. It had started in the yard—a shank made from a toothbrush handle, a debt unpaid, a look held too long—and now it was everywhere, spreading through the facility like fire through dry grass.

Inmates poured from breached cells, a tide of orange and improvised weapons. Mattresses burned in the common area, sending oily black smoke curling toward ceiling fans that spun uselessly, just stirring the haze. Men fought in clusters—fists, table legs, a broken mop handle sharpened to a point. The roar of voices blurred into something inhuman, less like men and more like the sound of a building screaming.

Near the showers, three inmates had cornered a guard, his baton already lost, his radio crackling unanswered pleas for backup that wouldn't come in time. He went down hard, boots finding ribs, and someone was shouting his name like that might still mean something in here.

Riot teams pushed through the smoke in formation, shields raised, pepper spray fogging the air into something that burned the eyes and throat alike. Rubber bullets cracked off concrete and flesh in equal measure. A guard swung his baton in wide arcs, connecting with a shoulder, a skull, anything that moved in orange. Blood ran into the grout lines on the floor, mixing with spilled bleach from a maintenance cart overturned in the scramble.

Above it all, the catwalks groaned with the weight of officers trying to regain the high ground, shouting orders that dissolved into the chaos below. Someone had gotten hold of a fire extinguisher and was using it like a club. Another inmate lay still near the stairs, no one stopping to check if he was breathing.

The lights flickered as the backup generator kicked in, casting everything in a sickly amber that made the smoke look like fog rolling through hell's own waiting room. And still it went on—the shouting, the cracking of batons, the wet sounds of violence that no training prepares you for—until exhaustion or reinforcement decided which side would still be standing when the smoke finally cleared.

# The Cleaning Ritual

The hotel room smelled like gun oil and the lavender air freshener that hadn't worked in years. Marcus sat cross-legged on the bed, a disassembled pistol spread across a white towel like surgical instruments. Across from him, Dani perched on the windowsill, running a whetstone along the edge of a knife with the patience of someone sharpening a pencil.

"I still think you're overcomplicating things," Marcus said, not looking up from the slide he was wiping down. "Garrotes. Cute. Theatrical. But you ever try one in a place with carpet? Nightmare."

"It's not about the carpet, Marcus, it's about the *intimacy*." Dani held the blade up to the lamplight, checking for nicks. "You want to know someone's heard your breathing before they go. That's connection."

"Connection." He snorted. "You sound like you're describing a first date."

"Aren't I?" She smirked, setting the knife down to pick up a cloth. "Look, the gun's fine. Efficient. Boring. It's a vending machine. Insert bullet, receive corpse. Where's the *craft*?"

"The craft is in not getting caught, which—correct me if I'm wrong—is sort of the entire job description."

"Sure, sure." She waved a hand. "But you've got no *signature*. Anyone can pull a trigger. I bet half our clients could do it themselves if they had the stomach."

Marcus finally looked up, raising an eyebrow. "And strangling someone with piano wire is a signature?"

"It's *elegant*." She said it like he'd insulted a relative. "There's a rhythm to it. You feel the moment they stop fighting. It's almost—"

"Romantic?"

"I was gonna say *musical*, but sure, go with your gut." She went back to polishing, the cloth squeaking faintly against steel. "What about poison? You ever tried poison?"

"Too slow. Too many variables. You poison a guy's drink, and suddenly he decides tonight's the night he switches to water. Whole plan's shot." He clicked the slide back into the pistol with a satisfying snap. "I respect the patience, though. Poison's for people who like waiting rooms."

"It's for people who like *certainty*." Dani held up the knife again, satisfied with the edge now. "Cyanide doesn't miss. Bullets miss. You ever miss, Marcus?"

"Once. In '09. Wind."

"Wind," she repeated, deadpan.

"It was windy."

"You're blaming weather for a miss."

"I'm *explaining* a miss. There's a difference." He set the gun down, finally satisfied, and reached for the cleaning solvent to cap it. "Besides, you've got your own embarrassing stories. Remember Lisbon?"

Dani's face soured instantly. "We don't talk about Lisbon."

"The guy *fought back*. With a lamp."

"He surprised me."

"You got beaned with a lamp, Dani."

"It was a *heavy* lamp." She pointed the knife at him for emphasis, then seemed to realize what she was doing and lowered it, laughing despite herself. "Okay, fine. Maybe garrotes have a downside. Maybe sometimes people fight back and ruin the *romance* of it."

"See, that's why I like guns. No romance required. Pop, done, dinner reservations at eight."

"You're so unsentimental."

"I'm *efficient*."

"You're *boring*."

"I'm *alive*, which is more than I can say for half the people who tried the intimate approach." He twirled the cleaning rod between his fingers like a tiny baton. "Besides, you talk about connection, but have you ever noticed how much faster the paperwork goes with a gun? Less mess. Less guilt. Less—"

"Soul," Dani finished, sheathing her now-gleaming knife with a satisfied click. "Yeah, yeah. I've heard the lecture."

They sat in silence a moment, the quiet hum of the air conditioner filling the space between them, weapons gleaming in the lamp light like trophies after a hunt that hadn't happened yet.

"You want pizza?" Marcus asked eventually, standing to stretch.

"Depends. Pepperoni or sausage?"

"Pepperoni's basic."

"Pepperoni's a *classic*, you absolute philistine." Dani hopped off the windowsill, knife already vanishing into a sheath at her hip. "Get the pizza. I'll start packing."

And just like that, the conversation shifted—weapons cleaned, philosophies debated, the night's work waiting just beyond the curtains, patient as ever.

The necromancer Vaelkrist stood at the center of the killing field, where three armies had bled into the same churned earth a decade past. Bones jutted from the soil like the rotted teeth of some vast buried beast. He had chosen this place for the density of the dead, for the way the ground itself seemed to hum with old, unfinished violence.

He began the working.

The words that left his mouth were not meant for human throats. They scraped against the air, syllables that bent the wrong way, vowels that tasted of copper and spoiled meat even to speak. Each one felt like a small violation—not of any law, but of *reality's* preference for things to remain as they were. The dead were supposed to stay dead. The magic knew this too, and it resisted him with a kind of nauseated reluctance, like flesh recoiling from a blade.

The first corpse rose wrong.

It had been a soldier once—armor still clinging in rusted plates to a torso gone concave with decay. The spine arched backward at an angle no living vertebrae should permit, joints popping with sounds like wet kindling as the thing folded itself upright. Its face had liquefied long ago, leaving a mask of bone-grey skin stretched taut over the skull, lips peeled back in a permanent rictus that exposed teeth black with rot. When it opened its mouth, no breath moved, yet sound came anyway—a dry, papery whisper that seemed to originate from everywhere and nowhere, as if the air itself were forced to carry a voice it found offensive.

More followed. They tore themselves from the mud in clusters, fingers first—skeletal digits breaching the soil like pale grubs—then forearms, shoulders, skulls trailing ropes of blackened sinew. The smell was a physical thing, a wall of sweet corruption that coated the tongue and clung to the lungs. Flies that had long since had nothing left to feast on swarmed anyway, drawn by instinct to flesh that should not move, should not *want* anything, yet shuffled forward with a horrible, hungry purpose.

Vaelkrist watched a woman's corpse claw free of the earth, her belly split and empty, the cavity packed with writhing wet shadow instead of organs—the magic filling the absence where life had been, an obscene parody of vitality. Her eyes, when they opened, held no light. They were simply *holes*, twin apertures into something that watched him with the flat, patient hatred of the truly dead.

# The Last Course

The wine was a Burgundy, '08, decanted an hour before service—long enough to breathe, not long enough to taste anything beyond the grape. I'd chosen it myself. Marcus always trusted my palate more than his own, which was, in the end, his most consistent flaw.

"You've gone quiet," he said, swirling the glass before he drank. "Cat got your tongue, or did you finally run out of opinions about my merger?"

"I'm savoring," I said. "Eat. The duck will go cold."

He cut into it obligingly—he always did what I suggested, in small things, which made the large betrayal easier to forgive himself for. The confit was perfect, the skin lacquered and crackling, and beneath it, dissolved into the reduction, the foxglove did its quiet work. Digitalis doesn't announce itself. It waits.

"This merger," he continued, oblivious, gesturing with his fork, "is going to make us both very comfortable. You understand that, don't you? Comfortable enough that none of this—" he waved at the apartment, the table, perhaps at me "—needs to matter anymore."

I watched his throat work as he swallowed. Twenty minutes, perhaps twenty-five. I'd given him enough.

By the time the second course arrived, he rubbed his eyes once, twice. "Strange," he said. "Lights seem brighter tonight."

"Do they?"

"Halos around the candles. Must be tired." He laughed, but it came out wrong, a beat too long. He pressed two fingers to his sternum, absent, the way men do when they assume indigestion.

I poured more wine. He drank it gratefully, not noticing his hand trembled faintly around the stem.

"You should see a doctor about that fatigue," I said. "You've mentioned it before."

"It's nothing." He blinked hard, twice, like a man trying to clear water from his eyes. "Did I tell you about Geneva? The deal—" He stopped. Pressed his palm flat against the table, as if to steady a room that had begun, ever so slightly, to tilt.

"Marcus?"

"Heart's doing something odd." He said it lightly, the way he said everything, as though the body were a subordinate that occasionally misbehaved but always, eventually, fell back in line. "Skipping. Or—racing. I can't tell."

"Drink some water."

He did. His hand shook now, openly, the glass clicking twice against his teeth before he set it down. Sweat had bloomed at his hairline, his collar. The color had gone from his face the way light leaves a room when a door swings shut.

"I think," he said, "I should sit somewhere else."

"You're sitting."

"I don't feel—" His eyes found mine, and for one unbearable second there was real fear in them, the particular fear of a man whose body has just informed him, irrevocably, that something is wrong. Not later. Now.

"I don't feel right," he finished, and his hand went to his chest properly this time, fingers curling into his shirt.

I did not move to help him. I watched the diaphragm in his neck flutter, watched his lips take on the faint blue tinge of a man whose heart has forgotten its rhythm, watched the duck congeal on his abandoned plate.

"Marcus," I said gently, the way you'd address someone already half gone, "you should have listened when I told you not to trust me with the wine."

He didn't hear it. By then, he wasn't hearing much of anything at all.

The sun hung low over the water, painting the waves the color of rust and old blood. Captain Verlaine stood with one boot propped on a coil of rope, watching the proceedings with the patient expression of a man who had done this before and would do it again.

The plank extended from the gunwale like an accusing finger, and at its end stood Thomas Hale, hands bound, shirt torn from the beating he'd taken when they'd dragged him up from the brig. Below, the water churned—not with the usual restless motion of the sea, but with something more deliberate. Dark shapes moved beneath the surface, unhurried, patient as the captain himself.

"You should've thought of sharks before you put a knife to my back, Mr. Hale," Verlaine said, not unkindly. "Walk on."

Hale's legs wouldn't obey at first. He stood frozen, staring down at the water where a fin broke the surface, sliced through it, vanished again. His breathing came in short, ragged pulls. The crew had gathered along the rail, faces unreadable, some looking away, others leaning forward with the unashamed hunger of men who needed reminding why mutiny was a word better left unspoken.

"Please—" Hale started, but the first mate's cutlass found the small of his back, a wordless argument that ended the conversation.

He walked. Each step bowed the wood beneath him, the plank groaning its complaint to the waves. His bound hands found no balance, and twice he swayed, breath catching, before forcing himself onward. The water below had gone still in a way that felt worse than the churning—a held breath, an audience waiting.

At the end of the plank, he stopped. Looked back once at the captain, who offered nothing—no mercy, no triumph, only the flat patience of consequence finally arrived.

"Go on, then," Verlaine said.

Hale didn't jump. The push came from behind, sudden and absolute, and his scream cut off as the water swallowed him.

For one heartbeat, nothing.

Then the sea convulsed. A gray shape rose half out of the water in a spray of foam gone instantly pink, and Hale's scream returned, higher now, a sound that didn't belong to words anymore. The crew flinched as one, though none looked away. The water boiled—three sharks, maybe four, drawn by blood and thrashing, their bodies cutting violent arcs beneath the surface. Once his arm broke free, reaching for the hull, fingers splayed, before something pulled him under with terrible finality.

The red spread wide across the water, and the frenzy did not last long after that. The sea quieted as suddenly as it had erupted, the fins dispersing, the surface smoothing back into its rusted, indifferent calm.

Verlaine turned from the rail before the water had even stilled.

"Let that be the only lesson needed," he said. "Back to your posts."

The crew dispersed in silence, and the ship sailed on, leaving nothing behind but a stain that the tide would erase by morning, as if the sea itself preferred to forget.

# The Weight of Water

The dripping started on a Tuesday.

Marcus first noticed it while reviewing quarterly reports, a soft *plink-plink-plink* that seemed to come from everywhere and nowhere. He checked the bathroom faucet. Dry. He checked the kitchen. Dry. But the sound followed him, patient as a held breath, until he poured himself a whiskey just to drown it out.

That night, he dreamed of the river. Of Elena's face beneath the surface, her dark hair fanning out like ink bleeding into water, her eyes open and accusing even as the current pulled her under. He woke gasping, sheets soaked through with sweat, and found wet footprints leading from his bed to the window.

Size seven. Elena's size.

"You're losing it," he told himself, scrubbing the floor with a towel until his knuckles bled. "She's gone. It's done."

But she wasn't gone. Not really.

She started appearing in mirrors first—just a flicker, there and gone, her face superimposed over his own reflection. Then she graduated to corners of rooms, standing motionless in shadow, water pooling at her feet and spreading across hardwood floors that remained, impossibly, dry. He'd blink and she'd be closer. Blink again and she'd be gone, leaving only that smell—river mud and decay—clinging to the air like a held grudge.

His coworkers began to notice. The way he flinched at puddles. The way he refused to drink from glasses, terrified of what might be floating in them. The way he'd suddenly freeze mid-sentence, eyes locked on something only he could see, his face draining of color as he whispered, "I'm sorry. I'm sorry. Please, I'm *sorry*—"

The dreams worsened. Elena would climb out of the river in slow, jerking movements, her movements all wrong, like a marionette with tangled strings. Water poured from her mouth in an endless stream as she crawled toward him across the muddy bank, fingers hooking into the earth, dragging herself forward with horrible, patient determination. *You held me down,* she'd gurgle, her voice thick with silt and rage. *You held me down and you watched.*

He started leaving the lights on. All of them. Every room blazing at 3 AM while he sat in the center of his living room, knees hugged to his chest, listening to water drip from a ceiling that showed no water damage.

Then came the night she stood at the foot of his bed.

Not a flicker. Not a trick of shadow. She stood there fully formed, skin grey and bloated, river water sluicing off her ruined dress in continuous sheets that vanished before hitting the floor. Her eyes—God, her eyes—held no anger now. Only a terrible, knowing patience, as if she had all the time in the world. As if death had taught her patience he could never comprehend.

"Please," he whispered. "Please, just leave me alone."

She tilted her head, water sloughing from her hair in dark ropes. When she spoke, her voice bubbled up like something rising from deep, stagnant water:

"*I can't leave. You put me inside you. I am the water in your lungs now.*"

She raised one waterlogged hand and pointed not at him, but *through* him—at something behind his own ribs, some drowning thing he'd carried since that night at the river, since he'd held her under and felt her stop fighting, felt the exact, terrible moment life left her body in a final desperate bubble of breath.

Marcus opened his mouth to scream.

Water poured out instead.

It kept coming—gallons, rivers, an ocean's worth—pouring from his throat as he convulsed on the bed, drowning from the inside while fully conscious, fully aware, fully *understanding* at last what he'd done. The room filled around him, dark water rising past the headboard, past the ceiling, and through it all, Elena watched with those patient, knowing eyes, waiting for him to finally, truly join her in the deep.

When his housekeeper found him three days later, the room was bone dry.

His lungs, the coroner noted with professional confusion, were completely filled with river water.

The kind found only forty miles away, in a current that had claimed exactly one body the previous spring—a young woman named Elena Castellanos, whose case had gone cold for lack of evidence, whose family still lit candles every Sunday, praying for the truth to surface.

It had, in its own way. Just not one anyone could explain.

Not a flicker. Not a trick of shadow. She stood there fully formed, skin grey and bloated, river water sluicing off her ruined dress in continuous sheets that vanished before hitting the floor. Her eyes—God, her eyes—held no anger now. Only a terrible, knowing patience, as if she had all the time in the world. As if death had taught her patience he could never comprehend.

"Please," he whispered. "Please, just leave me alone."

She tilted her head, water sloughing from her hair in dark ropes. When she spoke, her voice bubbled up like something rising from deep, stagnant water:

"I can't leave. You put me inside you. I am the water in your lungs now."

She raised one waterlogged hand and pointed not at him, but through him—at something behind his own ribs, some drowning thing he'd carried since that night at the river, since he'd held her under and felt her stop fighting, felt the exact, terrible moment life left her body in a final desperate bubble of breath.

Marcus opened his mouth to scream.

Water poured out instead.

It kept coming—gallons, rivers, an ocean's worth—pouring from his throat as he convulsed on the bed, drowning from the inside while fully conscious, fully aware, fully understanding at last what he'd done. The room filled around him, dark water rising past the headboard, past the ceiling, and through it all, Elena watched with those patient, knowing eyes, waiting for him to finally, truly join her in the deep.

When his housekeeper found him three days later, the room was bone dry.

His lungs, the coroner noted with professional confusion, were completely filled with river water.

The kind found only forty miles away, in a current that had claimed exactly one body the previous spring—a young woman named Elena Castellanos, whose case had gone cold for lack of evidence, whose family still lit candles every Sunday, praying for the truth to surface.

It had, in its own way. Just not one anyone could explain.

The body lay there like the city itself had finally given up pretending it was something other than what it was. Rotten to the bone, dressed up in chrome and ambition, but underneath—this. Always this.

I'd seen worse. I told myself that, the way you tell yourself any lie that gets you through the next sixty seconds. The blood had pooled and dried into a map of some country nobody wanted to visit, dark continents spreading across the concrete, and I thought about how the city did that too—spread its sickness slow, block by block, until you woke up one morning and your whole life was a bad neighborhood.

The smell hit different in the August heat. Copper and garbage and something sweeter underneath, the smell of meat starting to understand it was meat. Three days, maybe four. Long enough for the flies to set up permanent residence, long enough for whatever soul had lived in that body to pack its bags and leave the rent unpaid. The city was good at that. Eviction without notice. One day you're a person with a name and a coffee order and a girl who worries when you don't call, and the next you're inventory in some uniform's notebook, a case number, a problem for guys like me who'd stopped believing in solutions a long time ago.

Behind me, the buildings leaned in close, the way they always did at scenes like this, gray and patient and indifferent, tenements with windows like cataract eyes that had watched a thousand of these tableaus and would watch a thousand more. The city wasn't a place. It was an organism, and we were the cells it sloughed off when it didn't need us anymore. Skin cells. Dead skin on a corpse that called itself progress.

I crouched down, careful where I put my weight, and looked at what was left of the face. Somebody's kid. Somebody's bad decision, or somebody's bad luck, which down here amounted to the same thing wearing different clothes. The eyes were open, looking up at a sky the color of cigarette ash, like he was still waiting for the city to explain itself, to apologize, to admit that the postcards lied.

It never would. The city didn't apologize. It just kept rotting, slow and patient, building by building, soul by soul, and called the rot a skyline.

I straightened up, joints complaining like old plumbing, and lit a cigarette I didn't want, because some rituals you do anyway. The smoke curled up into that ash-gray sky and disappeared, the way everything down here eventually disappeared—into rumor, into paperwork, into the long patient digestion of a city that ate its own and never once said thank you.

Time to find out who did this. Not because it would matter. Because somebody had to pretend it did.

The fog made everything liminal, half-real, the kind of morning where sound traveled strangely and shapes resolved too late to matter. Mara had been running since the second siren, maybe four hours now, her lungs burning with that particular fire that comes right before the body starts shutting down options to save itself.

She'd made it to the old grain silos. That was something. Last season's runner from her block hadn't gotten past the highway.

The drone had clipped her twenty minutes back—not a kill-shot, just a marker round, a fluorescent tag burrowed into her shoulder so they'd always know where the prize was running. That was the cruelty of the Hunts. They didn't want it fast. The marker meant whoever drew her number could take their time.

She heard him before she saw him. Unhurried footsteps on gravel, a rhythm with no fear in it, no urgency. That was somehow worse than if he'd been sprinting.

"You picked a good line," the voice said, conversational, like they were neighbors meeting on a trail. "Most runners go for the river. Predictable. The silos—that showed some thought."

Mara pressed herself against rusted metal and didn't answer. Answering was for people who still believed talking could change an outcome.

"I'm going to find you in about ninety seconds," he continued. "I always do. So we don't have to make this ugly. I've seen ugly. It doesn't change the math."

She bolted anyway—not because she believed in the eighty seconds before that, but because stillness felt like consent. Her boots hit standing water, the silo's old drainage trench, and the sound betrayed her instantly.

He was there before she'd cleared the next row of pillars. Not even out of breath. Tall, unremarkable, wearing the kind of muted gray gear that made hunters interchangeable, anonymous, almost bureaucratic. He held the tracker-rifle loosely, like a man holding a clipboard, not a weapon.

"There she is."

Mara's hand found a length of pipe, useless and she knew it, but her body wasn't taking instructions anymore. He didn't even raise the rifle.

"You get one thing," he said. "Everyone does. A sentence. Some people scream. Some people pray. The smart ones say something I'll remember." He paused, almost respectful. "What's yours?"

She thought of every speech she might have written in her head over months of dreading this exact moment, and none of it came. Only her daughter's name surfaced, quiet and small, not meant for him at all.

"That's a good one," he said softly, and there was no cruelty in his voice, which was its own kind of horror. He raised the rifle—not the marker round this time. "Most people don't even get that far."

The shot was administrative. Quiet. The fog absorbed the sound like it absorbed everything else out here, like the silos had absorbed a hundred names before hers.

He walked to her body without hurry, knelt, and pressed his palm against the tag still glowing faintly in her shoulder. The transponder chimed once—claim registered, prize confirmed, leaderboard updated for the watching world that paid for mornings exactly like this one.

He stood, brushed gravel from his knee, and spoke into his collar mic with the flat satisfaction of a man closing out a routine task.

"Runner four-eleven secured. Moving to collection point."

Then he walked back into the fog the same way he'd come—unhurried, untroubled—already thinking, perhaps, of the next siren.

# The Shovel

The rain had stopped sometime before dawn, leaving the trench floor a soup of mud and things Tomas didn't want to name. He'd lost his rifle three minutes ago—or three hours, time had gone strange—when the German raiding party came over the top and into their line, and now he had nothing but the shovel.

It wasn't even his. He'd grabbed it off the wall where some quartermaster had hung it, all practical and ordinary, meant for digging latrines and reinforcing walls, not for what it was about to become.

The man who came around the traverse was younger than Tomas expected. That was the thing nobody told you—that the enemy would have a face, and the face would be afraid, and the fear would look exactly like your own.

There was no time for the rifle slung uselessly across the German's back. No time for words in any language. The man's eyes widened—recognition, calculation, the same animal arithmetic running behind both their skulls—and then they were both moving.

Tomas swung first. The shovel caught the German's raised forearm with a sound like wood splitting, and the man screamed, high and short, before he drove forward with his whole body, knocking Tomas back against the trench wall. Mud in his mouth. A knee somewhere near his ribs. Tomas's hands found the shovel's handle again on instinct alone, some animal part of his brain that had taken over completely now, the thinking part gone quiet and far away.

He swung again.

This time the blade caught the side of the man's head, and the sound was different—wetter, final—and the German went down sideways into the mud, one leg still kicking, kicking, like a dreaming dog.

Tomas stood over him. The rain had started again, fine as mist, and he could hear his own breathing, ragged and enormous in his ears, louder than the artillery still grumbling somewhere to the east. The German made a sound. Not a word. Just a sound, low and wrong, and his hand opened and closed in the mud as if reaching for something that wasn't there anymore.

Tomas hit him again. He didn't remember deciding to. His arms simply did it, lifting and falling, lifting and falling, until the sounds stopped and there was only the rain and his own heartbeat slamming against his ribs like something trying to escape.

He dropped the shovel. 

His hands were shaking—he noticed this distantly, as if observing someone else's hands. There was a warmth on his face that he understood, without looking, was not rain. He turned and vomited against the trench wall, his body rejecting what his mind couldn't yet process, heaving until there was nothing left and still heaving after that.

Down the line, the sounds of the raid were already fading—shouts in German growing distant, a few last shots, then the strange thick silence that always followed violence like a held breath finally released. Someone called his name. Pritchard, maybe, or Voss. He couldn't make himself answer.

He looked down at the man in the mud. Not a man anymore. A thing that had stopped being a man four minutes ago, when Tomas had needed it to stop, and would never start again no matter how long the war continued. The shovel lay beside him, ordinary, caked with mud and worse, waiting to be picked up again, cleaned, used tomorrow to dig a place for someone else to stand and bleed.

He thought: *I will remember this forever.*

He thought: *I have already started to forget his face.*

Both things were true, and he understood, crouched there in the mud with his hands shaking and his throat raw, that he had crossed into some country from which there was no clean road back. The war would end, someday. The trenches would fill in, or collapse, or simply be abandoned to grass and rain and time. But this—this single violent intimacy, this nearness of his hands to another man's dying—this would not end. This would live in him the way the shovel now lived in his hands, an object transformed by use into something it could never unbecome.

Above the trench line, the guns started again, indifferent, eternal. Tomas picked up the shovel. There was still a war to dig through.

# The Square

The bell tower struck noon as they led him up the wooden steps. He couldn't have been more than sixteen, wrists bound with the same rough rope used for cattle, his oversized coat swallowing his thin frame.

The crowd packed the square—mothers with children on their shoulders, vendors who'd paused their carts, old men who came every Thursday because executions were the only theater left in their lives. A child near the front asked her father what the boy had done.

"Stole bread," the father said. "Don't stare."

She stared anyway.

The magistrate read the charge in a flat, administrative voice, the words "theft of property, one loaf, value assessed at four coins" carrying the same weight as a weather report. Somewhere in the crowd, a woman began crying—not loudly, just a steady leak of grief she tried to hide behind her shawl. Her neighbor shifted away from her, uncomfortable, glancing around to see who'd noticed.

Most faces showed nothing at all. This was Thursday. Thursday was executions.

A vendor selling roasted chestnuts called out his prices, undisturbed, his voice overlapping with the magistrate's final words. Two boys near the fountain were betting on how long it would take—they'd seen enough of these to have opinions now, to treat it like weather, like sport.

The teenager's eyes moved across the crowd once, searching for something—a familiar face, a sign of mercy, anything—before settling on nothing in particular. He'd stopped struggling somewhere between the jail and the gallows. His lips moved. Maybe a prayer. Maybe just his mother's name.

When it was over, the crowd dispersed with the particular efficiency of people returning to errands. The chestnut vendor did brisk business. The crying woman was already gone, swallowed into the current of bodies heading back to work, back to market, back to lives that required bread of their own.

By evening, no one mentioned it. By the next morning, the square hosted a different kind of crowd, haggling over the price of vegetables, stepping around the spot where the platform had stood, already cleared away, already forgotten—until next Thursday.

---

This scene aims to show how systems of cruelty become normalized through repetition—the true horror often resides not in the act itself, but in the mundane indifference that surrounds it.
